# Choosing Your Eyes {#sec-sensors}

::: {.chapter-goal}
#### In this chapter
The satellites you will actually use, what each one is genuinely good at, and a decision procedure for picking between them that does not reduce to using whichever one you used last time.
:::

## No sensor is the right sensor

A recurring pattern in early career work is loyalty to one satellite. Someone learns Sentinel-2, gets good at it, and then applies it to a question that needs a thirty year archive or a thermal band or a signal that penetrates cloud. The map that results is not wrong so much as unable to answer the question that was asked.

The professional habit is the reverse. Start from the question, derive the requirement, then pick the sensor. This chapter gives you enough about each platform to do that.

## The optical workhorses

| | Landsat 8 and 9 | Sentinel-2 |
|---|---|---|
| Visible and NIR | 30 m | 10 m |
| Red edge | none | 3 bands at 20 m |
| Shortwave infrared | 30 m | 20 m |
| Thermal | 100 m, resampled to 30 m | none |
| Revisit, full constellation | 8 days | 5 days |
| Archive begins | 1972 for the programme, 2013 for Landsat 8 | 2015 |
| Radiometric depth | 12 bit | 12 bit |
| Swath | 185 km | 290 km |

: The two optical programmes compared {.striped}

**Landsat** is the historical record. Nothing else on this list can tell you what a landscape looked like in 1990, and for baselines, long term trends and any claim about change over decades, that is decisive. It also carries the only thermal sensor in this group. Its weakness is the 30 metre pixel, which cannot resolve a smallholder plot or a narrow mangrove fringe.

**Sentinel-2** is the modern default for detail. Ten metre pixels, red edge bands, five day revisit. If your question is about the present and about features smaller than a hectare, this is the answer. Its weakness is the short archive: it simply cannot speak to anything before 2015.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common failure: the resolution that is not there
A Sentinel-2 composite drawn at 10 metres looks like it has 10 metre information in every band. It does not. Only four bands are natively 10 metre: blue, green, red and the wide near infrared B8. The red edge bands, the narrow near infrared B8A and both shortwave infrared bands are natively 20 metre, and the atmospheric bands are 60 metre. Earth Engine will happily resample all of them to 10 metres when you combine them, which produces an image that displays at 10 metres and carries 20 metre information in most of its bands. This does not make an analysis wrong, but it does make claims about detecting 10 metre features from a shortwave infrared index untrue.
:::

## Radar

Sentinel-1 works on an entirely different principle. It emits microwave pulses and measures the fraction scattered back, so it needs no sunlight and passes through cloud with no meaningful loss.

What comes back depends on three surface properties.

**Roughness relative to the wavelength.** A surface smooth at the scale of the wavelength, calm water, reflects the pulse away from the sensor and appears very dark. A rough surface scatters in all directions, including back, and appears bright.

**Geometry.** Vertical structures beside a horizontal surface, tree trunks standing in water, produce a double bounce: the pulse hits the water, reflects to the trunk, and returns along its incoming path. This is extremely bright and it is characteristic of flooded forest, which is exactly what a mangrove is at high tide.

**Moisture.** Water raises the dielectric constant of a material, increasing backscatter. Wet soil is brighter than dry soil.

Sentinel-1 transmits and receives in two polarisation combinations, and they carry different information. **VV**, vertical out and vertical back, responds mostly to surface scattering and is good for water and bare ground. **VH**, vertical out and horizontal back, only returns energy that has been depolarised by multiple scattering inside a volume, which makes it the canopy volume channel and the one that correlates with biomass.

::: {.callout-note}
## Concept: wavelength determines what the radar sees
Sentinel-1 is C band, around 5.6 centimetres. That interacts mainly with leaves and small branches, so it senses the upper canopy.

ALOS PALSAR is L band, around 23 centimetres. Longer waves pass through foliage and interact with trunks and large branches, so L band reaches further into and through the canopy and correlates better with total above ground biomass. It is also less prone to saturating in dense forest.

The practical implication for mangroves: C band tells you about canopy condition, L band tells you about structure and biomass, and using both is not redundancy. Chapter [-@sec-sar] stacks them together.
:::

Radar carries one cost that optical does not: speckle. Because the return is the coherent sum of many scatterers within a resolution cell, the signal has a grainy multiplicative noise that is inherent to the physics rather than a sensor defect. It must be filtered, and Chapter [-@sec-sar] covers how without destroying the edges you care about.

## The supporting cast

**ALOS World 3D, 30 metre.** The elevation model this book defaults to. Better vertical accuracy than SRTM in most of Asia. Note that it is a surface model, so over forest it records canopy top rather than ground.

**SRTM, 90 and 30 metre.** The long standing global default, acquired in 2000. Still perfectly usable, and its age matters only if your terrain has changed.

**GEDI.** Spaceborne LiDAR from the International Space Station, sampling canopy height in footprints rather than wall to wall coverage. You cannot map with it directly. You calibrate against it, which is what Chapter [-@sec-regression] does.

**Google satellite embeddings.** Not a sensor. A learned representation derived from many sensors, 64 dimensions per 10 metre pixel per year. Chapter [-@sec-embeddings].

## A decision procedure

Work through these in order. The first constraint that binds usually determines the answer.

**Does the question require history before 2015?** Then Landsat, and accept 30 metres.

**Does it require surface temperature?** Then Landsat, since nothing else here has a thermal band.

**Are the features smaller than about half a hectare?** Then Sentinel-2, or commercial imagery if smaller than about 100 square metres.

**Is cloud cover so persistent that a year of optical data leaves holes?** Then radar must be in the stack, not as a supplement but as a primary source.

**Does the question concern vertical structure or biomass?** Then radar, preferably both C and L band, and GEDI for calibration if you need absolute height.

**Is it a broad land cover baseline with limited training data and no need for sub annual timing?** Then satellite embeddings will likely outperform anything you assemble by hand, in a fraction of the effort.

## Fusion, and when it is worth the cost

Combining sensors nearly always improves accuracy, and it always increases complexity. The judgement is whether the improvement is worth the maintenance.

The case where fusion is clearly justified is mangrove mapping, because the confusion that limits accuracy is between mangrove and other dense broadleaf forest, and optical data alone cannot resolve it. The separating information is physical rather than spectral: mangroves sit within a narrow elevation band above sea level, and they stand in water, which produces a double bounce radar signature that terrestrial forest does not have. Adding elevation and radar does not marginally improve the map. It fixes the specific error that was capping its accuracy.

The case where fusion is not justified is adding bands because they exist. Every band you add costs computation, adds a failure mode, and dilutes the classifier's attention. Chapter [-@sec-supervised] covers reading feature importance to find out which bands are earning their place, and Chapter [-@sec-sampling] covers what to do about the ones that are not.

::: {.callout-tip}
## From the field
Before building a fusion stack, run the classification on optical alone and record the confusion matrix. Then you know which specific class pair is failing, and you can add the one data source that addresses that pair. Adding everything at once and finding accuracy improved by three points tells you nothing about why.
:::

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. For your own study area, write down the question, then work the decision procedure above and record which constraint bound first.
2. Load the same date over your area from Landsat 9 and Sentinel-2. Zoom to a feature roughly 20 metres across. Describe what the 30 metre product loses.
3. Load a Sentinel-1 scene over a coastal area at high tide and at low tide. Find the double bounce signature.
4. Look up the tide state at the acquisition time of the Sentinel-2 scene you plan to use as a baseline. Note it in your method description now, before you forget.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

**1.** Example: "Has the mangrove fringe of the Mahakam delta retreated since 1995?" The first binding constraint is history before 2015, so Landsat at 30 m is the answer, with Sentinel-2 added only for the recent detail. If your question were "which ponds were dug last month", the first binding constraint would be feature size (under half a hectare) and the answer Sentinel-2, with Sentinel-1 if cloud blocks the month. Record the constraint, not just the sensor: it is your justification in the methods.

**2.** At 30 m a 20 m feature covers less than one pixel, so it is mixed with its surroundings: a narrow road, a canal or a two-row mangrove fringe becomes a soft blur or disappears, edges move by up to a pixel, and a small pond shows as a slightly darker pixel rather than open water. Sentinel-2's 10 m bands (B2, B3, B4, B8) show its shape. Remember the warning in this chapter: Sentinel-2's red edge and SWIR bands are 20 m, so the gain is only in the four 10 m bands.

**3.** At high tide the water under the trees creates double bounce: the mangrove looks very bright in VV and often in VH, brighter than dry forest inland, while the open water beside it is dark. At low tide the mud is exposed and the bright return weakens, so the contrast between fringe and inland forest drops. Pick two Sentinel-1 dates and check the tide tables for their times; the brightness change in the fringe, with no change inland, is the signature.

**4.** Write the acquisition time in local time and the tide height from a tide table or a tide model for the nearest port, for example "Sentinel-2, 2024-08-14 10:24 WITA, tide +1.8 m (high)". This matters because the visible mangrove edge and the mudflat area change with the tide; a baseline taken at low tide and a monitoring image at high tide will show loss that never happened.
:::
